reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine / Fishman's Pulmonary Diseases and Disorders
clinicalPearls: A clinical-pathological syndrome, not a single disease, presenting with breathlessness, cough, and diffuse alveolar infiltrates, often with hypoxaemia
Haemoptysis may be strikingly absent in up to a third of cases, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis
A falling haematocrit together with new diffuse infiltrates should raise suspicion of alveolar haemorrhage
The diagnostic hallmark on bronchoalveolar lavage is progressively bloodier fluid on sequential aliquots, and later haemosiderin-laden macrophages
Mechanistically it falls into three groups: pulmonary capillaritis (pauci-immune or immune), bland haemorrhage without inflammation, and haemorrhage associated with diffuse alveolar damage
Capillaritis is commonly due to ANCA-associated vasculitis or anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease and is frequently accompanied by a pulmonary-renal syndrome
The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide is characteristically raised acutely because intra-alveolar blood binds inhaled carbon monoxide
Immunosuppression is the mainstay for immune capillaritis, alongside supportive respiratory care and treatment of any underlying cause
reference.pathophysiology: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage results from disruption of the alveolar-capillary basement membrane, allowing red cells to flood the alveolar spaces. Three broad mechanisms are recognised. In pulmonary capillaritis there is neutrophilic inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis of the alveolar capillaries, most often from ANCA-associated vasculitis or anti-glomerular basement membrane disease. In bland haemorrhage the capillaries bleed without inflammation, as in coagulopathy, mitral stenosis, or idiopathic pulmonary haemosiderosis. In the third group, haemorrhage accompanies diffuse alveolar damage from infection, drugs, or toxins. Extravasated blood is phagocytosed by macrophages, which accumulate haemosiderin over the ensuing days.
additionalDifferentials: Diffuse pneumonia or acute respiratory distress syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Bronchoalveolar lavage with sequential aliquots showing progressively bloodier return and haemosiderin-laden macrophages
ANCA, anti-GBM antibody, antinuclear antibody, and complement testing to define an immune cause
Urinalysis and renal function to detect an associated glomerulonephritis (pulmonary-renal syndrome)
Full blood count and coagulation studies, noting a falling haematocrit
High-resolution CT showing diffuse ground-glass opacity and consolidation
Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide, which is typically elevated during active bleeding
redFlags: Rapidly progressive hypoxaemic respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support
Concurrent acute kidney injury suggesting a pulmonary-renal vasculitic syndrome
Falling haematocrit with expanding infiltrates indicating ongoing bleeding
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on the underlying cause and speed of treatment; immune capillaritis can respond well to prompt immunosuppression, but severe or recurrent haemorrhage, especially with renal involvement, carries significant morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because haemoptysis is absent
Mistaking the infiltrates for pneumonia or pulmonary oedema and missing an underlying vasculitis
Failing to check renal function and urinalysis for an associated glomerulonephritis
Overlooking the diagnostic value of sequential bronchoalveolar lavage aliquots and a raised carbon monoxide transfer factor
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Initiate prompt high-dose corticosteroids for suspected immune-mediated capillaritis, with additional immunosuppression such as cyclophosphamide or rituximab
Add plasma exchange for anti-GBM Goodpasture disease and severe ANCA-associated vasculitis, particularly with renal involvement
Support gas exchange with supplemental oxygen and mechanical ventilation when hypoxaemia is severe
Correct coagulopathy and treat bland-haemorrhage causes such as raised pulmonary venous pressure
Withdraw offending drugs or toxins and treat any underlying infection driving diffuse alveolar damage
Monitor haematocrit, oxygenation and infiltrates and manage in intensive care during active bleeding
Coordinate care with respiratory medicine, rheumatology and nephrology and screen for an associated glomerulonephritis
